a: The periodic table arranges all known elements by atomic number (protons). Columns share similar properties, like the noble gases on the far right. There are 118 confirmed elements.
more: Hydrogen is 1, carbon 6, oxygen 8, iron 26, gold 79.

q: how does the water cycle work
a: Water evaporates from oceans and lakes, rises and cools into clouds (condensation), falls as rain or snow (precipitation), and flows back to the sea through rivers and the ground.
more: The sun drives the whole cycle.

a: Energy is the ability to do work. Kinetic energy is energy of motion, potential energy is stored energy like a ball held up high. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.
more: Other forms: heat, light, chemical, electrical, nuclear.

a: 1) An object keeps moving or staying still unless a force acts on it. 2) Force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma). 3) Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
more: This is why seatbelts matter: your body wants to keep moving when the car stops.

a: Einstein's special relativity says the speed of light is constant and that time and space change with speed. E = mc² says mass and energy are equivalent. General relativity says gravity is the bending of space and time by mass.
more: GPS satellites must correct for relativity to stay accurate.

a: Quantum mechanics describes the tiny world of atoms and particles, where things act like both waves and particles and only probabilities can be predicted. Quantum computers use qubits that can be in several states at once to solve certain problems faster.
more: Transistors in your phone rely on quantum physics.

a: The Big Bang theory says the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since. Evidence includes the expansion of galaxies and the cosmic microwave background.
more: It describes how the universe grew, not what caused it.

a: A vaccine shows your immune system a harmless piece or weakened form of a germ so it learns to recognize it. If the real germ shows up later your body responds fast.
more: Herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated.

a: Bacteria are living single cells, and many are helpful. Viruses are much smaller, need a host cell to reproduce, and are not clearly alive. Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses.
more: Your gut has trillions of helpful bacteria.

q: how does the immune system work
a: The immune system defends your body. White blood cells find and destroy germs, and antibodies tag invaders. It remembers past infections so the next response is faster.
more: Sleep, food and exercise help it work well.

a: The cell is the basic unit of life. Key parts: nucleus (holds DNA), mitochondria (make energy), membrane (the boundary), and in plants chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a cell wall.
more: Your body has around 30 trillion cells.

a: Mitochondria are the parts of a cell that turn food into usable energy (ATP). That is why they are called the powerhouse of the cell.
more: They have their own small set of DNA.

a: An element is one kind of atom, like oxygen. A molecule is atoms bonded together, and a compound is a molecule made of different elements, like water (H2O).
more: Mixtures are not bonded, like salt dissolved in water.

a: pH measures how acidic something is from 0 to 14. Below 7 is acid (lemon juice), 7 is neutral (pure water), above 7 is base (soap, bleach).
more: Each step on the scale is a factor of ten.

a: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into new substances. Signs: gas bubbles, color change, heat or light, or a solid forming. Mass is conserved, nothing is lost.
more: Rusting and cooking are chemical reactions.

a: Sunlight contains all colors. Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths much more than red, so blue light reaches your eyes from every direction. At sunset the light travels through more air and the blue is scattered away, leaving red and orange.
more: This is called Rayleigh scattering.

a: Rivers wash tiny amounts of minerals and salts from rocks into the sea. Water evaporates but the salt stays, so over millions of years the ocean became salty.
more: About 3.5% of seawater is salt.

a: Seasons come from Earth's 23.5 degree tilt, not its distance from the sun. When your half of Earth tilts toward the sun you get summer, longer days and more direct light.
more: When it is summer in the north it is winter in the south.

q: why does the moon change shape
a: The moon does not change shape. We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth. The cycle is about 29.5 days: new, crescent, quarter, gibbous, full, and back.
more: Waxing means growing, waning means shrinking.

a: Tides are caused mostly by the moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans, with the sun adding to it. Most coasts get two high tides and two low tides a day.
more: Spring tides, the biggest ones, happen at full and new moon.

a: A solar eclipse is when the moon passes between the sun and Earth and blocks the sun. A lunar eclipse is when Earth passes between the sun and moon and its shadow falls on the moon.
more: Never look at the sun during a solar eclipse without proper eclipse glasses.

a: In order from the sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Mercury to Mars are rocky, Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
more: Pluto is a dwarf planet.

a: A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity. Our galaxy is the Milky Way, a spiral with hundreds of billions of stars, and the sun is one of them.
more: The nearest large galaxy is Andromeda.

a: A star is a giant ball of gas that shines by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. Stars form in clouds of gas and dust. Small ones fade quietly, massive ones end as supernovae and can leave neutron stars or black holes.
more: Our sun is about 4.6 billion years old, roughly halfway through its life.

a: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet because it has not cleared its orbit of other objects. It is still a real world with moons and mountains.
more: Other dwarf planets: Ceres, Eris, Haumea, Makemake.

a: Mars is the fourth planet, the red planet, colored by iron oxide. It has a thin atmosphere, the tallest volcano in the solar system (Olympus Mons), and evidence of ancient water. A day is about 24.6 hours.
more: Several rovers explore it, including Curiosity and Perseverance.

a: The moon is about 384,400 km (238,855 miles) from Earth on average. Light takes about 1.3 seconds to get there.
more: Apollo astronauts took around three days to reach it.

a: Earthquakes happen when tectonic plates that were stuck suddenly slip along a fault, releasing energy as seismic waves. Magnitude measures the size.
more: Most happen along plate edges like the Pacific Ring of Fire.

a: A volcano is an opening where molten rock (magma) reaches the surface as lava, ash and gas. Pressure from gas builds up underground and can cause eruptions.
more: Many sit above where plates meet or over hot spots.

a: Earth's outer shell is split into plates that slowly move a few centimeters a year. Where they collide, separate or slide past each other we get mountains, ocean trenches, volcanoes and earthquakes.
more: Pangaea was a supercontinent that broke apart about 200 million years ago.

a: Weather is what the atmosphere does today or this week. Climate is the average weather of a region over about 30 years or more.
more: One cold day does not disprove climate change.

a: Warm air rises and cools. When it cools enough, its water vapor condenses onto tiny particles and forms droplets, which we see as clouds.
more: Different heights and conditions give cumulus, stratus and cirrus clouds.

a: A rainbow forms when sunlight enters raindrops, bends, reflects inside and bends again, splitting into colors. You need the sun behind you and rain in front.
more: The order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

a: Lightning is a huge spark of static electricity released between clouds or from cloud to ground. It heats the air so fast that it expands explosively, which we hear as thunder.
more: Count the seconds between flash and bang, every 3 seconds is about 1 km.

a: Sound is vibrations that travel as waves through air, water or solids. It cannot travel through a vacuum. In air it moves at about 343 meters per second.
more: It is faster in water and much faster in steel.

a: Temperature measures how fast the particles in something are moving on average. Heat is the energy that flows from a hotter thing to a colder one.
more: A bathtub of warm water holds more heat than a cup of boiling water.

a: Magnetism is a force from moving electric charges. Magnets have two poles, north and south. Opposites attract and the same poles repel. Earth itself is a giant magnet, which is why compasses work.
more: Electricity and magnetism are two sides of electromagnetism.

a: A battery turns chemical energy into electricity. Chemical reactions push electrons from one terminal through your device to the other. Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable because the reaction can be reversed.
more: Voltage is the push, current is the flow.

a: Solar panels use photovoltaic cells that release electrons when sunlight hits them, producing electric current. An inverter converts it to the AC power your home uses.
more: Panels still produce some power on cloudy days.

a: Nuclear power plants split heavy atoms like uranium (fission) to release heat that makes steam and electricity. It is low in carbon emissions. Fusion joins light atoms like the sun does and is still being researched.
more: Waste storage and cost are the main challenges.

a: Renewable energy comes from sources that replenish: sun, wind, water, geothermal and biomass. Non-renewable ones like coal, oil and gas take millions of years to form and run out.
more: Storage is the main challenge for solar and wind.

a: The speed of sound in air is about 343 meters per second (1,235 km/h or 767 mph) at 20 degrees Celsius.
more: Mach 1 is the speed of sound.

a: Density is how much mass is packed into a space: density = mass / volume. Things denser than water sink, less dense ones float.
more: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.

a: Friction is the force that resists sliding between two surfaces, which turns motion into heat. Momentum is mass times velocity, how hard something is to stop.
more: Heavier and faster means more momentum.

a: Entropy measures disorder. The second law says that in a closed system entropy tends to increase, which is why heat flows from hot to cold and a broken cup does not fix itself.
more: It is also why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

a: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen, the left side pumps it to the rest of the body. It beats about 100,000 times a day.
more: Four chambers: two atria on top, two ventricles below.

a: The brain is made of about 86 billion neurons that send electrical and chemical signals. It controls thought, movement, memory, emotion and automatic things like breathing.
more: Different regions specialize, but they work together.

a: Adults have 206 bones. Babies are born with about 300, and many fuse as they grow. The smallest bone is the stapes in the ear, the largest is the femur.
more: Bones also make blood cells in the marrow.

a: The main blood groups are A, B, AB and O, each either Rh positive or negative. O negative can be given to almost anyone, AB positive can receive from anyone.
more: Your type is set by genes from your parents.

a: Digestion starts in the mouth with chewing and enzymes, food goes through the esophagus to the stomach where acid breaks it down, then the small intestine absorbs nutrients and the large intestine absorbs water.
more: It takes roughly 24 to 72 hours.

a: Sleep lets the brain clear waste, store memories and the body repair itself. Lack of sleep hurts mood, focus and health. Teens need about 8 to 10 hours, adults 7 to 9.
more: Dreams mostly happen in REM sleep.

a: Scientists are not certain. Dreams are linked to memory processing and emotions, mostly during REM sleep, when the brain is very active.
more: Most dreams are forgotten within minutes of waking.

a: DNA is the double-stranded molecule that stores genetic instructions. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. RNA is a single-stranded copy that carries those instructions out to build proteins.
more: You get half your DNA from each parent.

a: Most scientists agree an asteroid about 10 km wide hit Earth near Mexico 66 million years ago, causing fires, a long cold darkness and mass extinction. Birds are living dinosaurs that survived.
more: The crater is called Chicxulub.

a: An ecosystem is all the living things and non-living parts of an area interacting. A food chain shows who eats whom: producers (plants) are eaten by herbivores, which are eaten by carnivores. Decomposers recycle everything.
more: Remove one species and the whole web can change.

a: The ozone layer is a part of the atmosphere that absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet light. Chemicals called CFCs damaged it, and a global agreement (the Montreal Protocol) has let it slowly recover.
more: It is one of the biggest environmental success stories.

a: The scientific method: ask a question, research, make a testable hypothesis, run an experiment, analyze the results, and share them. A hypothesis is an educated guess that can be proven wrong.
more: Good science welcomes being wrong.

a: Wings are shaped so air moving over them creates lower pressure above and higher below, and they also push air downward. This produces lift. Engines give thrust to overcome drag, and lift beats weight.
more: Four forces: lift, weight, thrust, drag.

a: Your device asks a DNS server for the site's address, connects to that server through your internet provider, and sends an HTTP request. The server sends back HTML, CSS and JS and your browser draws the page.
more: Data travels in small packets that can take different routes.

a: GPS satellites broadcast their position and the exact time. Your phone measures how long each signal took to arrive from at least four satellites and calculates where you are.
more: It needs a clear view of the sky.

a: A prime is a number greater than 1 divisible only by 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.
In a right triangle, a squared plus b squared equals c squared, where c is the longest side.
Probability is how likely something is, from 0 to 1. The chance of heads on a fair coin is 1/2, or 0.5.
A derivative is the rate of change of a function, like speed is the rate of change of position. Integrals add up change, like distance from speed.
Gravity is the attraction between masses. On Earth it pulls things down at about 9.8 meters per second squared.
Light travels about 299,792 km per second, roughly 186,000 miles per second.
DNA is the molecule that stores genetic instructions, a twisted ladder made of four bases: A, T, C and G.
A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape once it crosses the event horizon.
Plants turn sunlight, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen using chlorophyll in their leaves.
The solar system has 8 planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Jupiter is the largest planet. You could fit over 1,300 Earths inside it.
About 4.5 billion years old.
The sun is a star made mostly of hydrogen. Its surface is about 5,500 C and its core about 15 million C.
An atom is the tiny building block of matter with a nucleus of protons and neutrons and electrons around it. Atoms bond to form molecules like water, H2O.
Matter is mainly solid, liquid or gas, depending on how fast its particles move. Heat turns solid to liquid to gas.
Evolution is how species change over generations. Natural selection means traits that help survival get passed on more often.
Electricity is the flow of electrons through a conductor. Voltage pushes, current is the flow, and resistance slows it.
Climate change is the long-term warming of Earth, mainly from burning fossil fuels that release greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide.
Thomas Edison made the first practical lightbulb in 1879. Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876.

q: what is a variable in math
a: Algebra uses letters for unknown numbers. To solve x + 3 = 7, do the same thing to both sides: subtract 3, so x = 4.
Pi is about 3.14159. Area = pi times radius squared. Circumference = 2 times pi times radius.
For ax^2 + bx + c = 0, x = (-b plus or minus the square root of (b^2 - 4ac)) divided by 2a.
To add fractions, give them the same bottom number (common denominator), then add the tops. 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
